source_text: Οἴεται δὲ τερατείαν εἶναι καὶ τὸν σεισμὸν καὶ τὸν σκότον· περὶ ὧν κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν ἐν τοῖς ἀνωτέρω ἀπελογησάμεθα, παραθέμενοι τὸν Φλέγοντα ἱστορήσαντα κατὰ τὸν χρόνον τοῦ πάθους τοῦ σωτῆρος τοιαῦτα ἀπηντηκέναι. καὶ ὅτι ζῶν μὲν οὐκ ἐπήρκεσεν ἑαυτῷ, νεκρὸς δ᾿ ἀνέστη καὶ τὰ σημεῖα τῆς κολάσεως ἔδειξεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς καὶ τὰς χεῖρας ὡς ἦσαν πεπερονημέναι. καὶ πυνθανόμεθα αὐτοῦ, τί τὸ ἐπήρκεσεν ἑαυτῷ; εἰ μὲν γὰρ πρὸς ἀρετὴν. φήσομεν ὅτι καὶ πάνυ γε ἐπήρκεσεν· οὐδὲν γὰρ ἄτοπον οὔτ᾿ ἐφθέγξατο οὔτ᾿ ἐποίησεν, ἀλλ᾿ ἀληθῶς „ὡς πρόβατον ἐπὶ σφαγὴν ἤχθη. καὶ ὡς ἀμνὸς ἐναντίον τοῦ κείροντος ἄφωνος“· καὶ μαρτυρεῖ τὸ εὐαγγέλιον ὅτι „οὕτως οὐκ“ ἤνοιξε „τὸ στόμα αὐτοῦ.“ εἰ δὲ τὸ ἐπήρκεσεν ἀπὸ τῶν μέσων καὶ σωματικῶν λαμβάνει, φαμὲν ὅτι ἀπεδείξαμεν ἐκ τῶν εὐαγγελίων ὅτι ἑκὼν ἐπὶ ταῦτ᾿ ἐλήλυθεν. εἶθ᾿ ἑξῆς τούτοις εἰπὼν τὰ ἀπὸ τοῦ εὐαγγελίου, ὅτι τὰ σημεῖα τῆς κολάσεως ἔδειξεν ἀναστὰς ἐκ νεκρῶν καὶ τὰς χεῖρας ὡς ἦσαν πεπερονημέναι, πυνθάνεται καὶ λέγει· τίς τοῦτο εἶδε: καὶ τὰ περὶ Μαρίας τῆς Μαγδαληνῆς διαβάλλων ἀναγραφομένης ἑωρακέναι εἶπε· γυνὴ πάροιστρος. ὥς φατε. καὶ ἐπεὶ μὴ μόνη αὕτη ἀναγέγραπται ἑωρακέναι ἀναστάντα τὸν Ἰησοῦν ἀλλὰ καὶ ἄλλοι. καὶ ταῦτα κακηγορῶν ὁ Κέλσου Ἰουδαῖός φησι· καὶ εἴ τις ἄλλος τῶν ἐκ τῆς αὐτῆς γοητείας.
pass_a_gloss: He supposes (οἴομαι) that both the earthquake (σεισμός) and the darkness (σκότος) are a marvel-tale (τερατεία); about which, as far as possible, we made a defence (ἀπολογέομαι) in the earlier parts, setting out Phlegon who recorded that such things happened at the time of the passion (πάθος) of the Saviour (σωτήρ). And that ‘living he did not help (ἐπαρκέω) himself, but dead he rose and showed the marks (σημεῖα) of the punishment (κόλασις) and the hands, how they had been pierced (περονάω), Jesus.’ And we inquire of him, what is ‘helped himself’? If with respect to virtue (ἀρετή), we shall say that he very much helped; for he neither uttered nor did anything out of place (ἄτοπον), but truly ‘as a sheep to slaughter he was led, and as a lamb before the shearer voiceless (ἄφωνος)’; and the Gospel bears witness (μαρτυρέω) that ‘thus he did not open his mouth.’ But if he takes ‘helped’ from the intermediate (μέσα, indifferent) and bodily (σωματικά) things, we say that we have shown from the Gospels that willingly (ἑκών) he came to these things. Then next, having said the things from the Gospel, that he showed the marks of the punishment having risen from the dead and the hands how they had been pierced, he asks and says: ‘Who saw this?’ And slandering (διαβάλλω) the things about Mary Magdalene, recorded to have seen, he said: ‘A frenzied (πάροιστρος) woman, as you say.’ And since not she alone is recorded to have seen Jesus risen but others too, reviling (κακηγορέω) these also Celsus’s Jew says: ‘and if any other of those from the same sorcery (γοητεία).’
pass_b_english: He thinks that both the earthquake and the darkness are a marvellous tale (Matthew 27:45, 51). We made our defence about these earlier, as far as we could, citing Phlegon, who recorded that such things occurred at the time of the Saviour’s passion. He also says that “while he was alive Jesus did not help himself, but when dead he rose and showed the marks of his punishment, and how his hands had been pierced” (John 20:20, 27).

We ask him: what does “helped himself” mean? If it refers to virtue, we shall say that he helped himself very much indeed. For he neither said nor did anything improper; but truly “he was led as a sheep to the slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer is silent” (Isaiah 53:7), and the Gospel testifies that “so he did not open his mouth” (Isaiah 53:7; Matthew 27:12–14). But if he takes “helped himself” in the sense of things indifferent and bodily, we say that we have shown from the Gospels that he came to these things of his own will.

Next, after stating what comes from the Gospel, that on rising from the dead he showed the marks of his punishment and how his hands had been pierced, he asks: “Who saw this?” And slandering the account of Mary Magdalene, who is recorded to have seen him (John 20:11–18), he said: “A frenzied woman, as you say.” And since she is not the only one recorded to have seen Jesus risen, but others too, Celsus’s Jew slanders these as well, and says: “and anyone else involved in the same sorcery.”

choices.why: Restored the subject ὁ Ἰησοῦς in Celsus’s words (‘Jesus did not help himself’), which had been dropped.
τῶν ἐκ τῆς αὐτῆς γοητείας: ‘whoever else came from the same sorcery’ to ‘anyone else involved in the same sorcery’ (εἴ τις ἄλλος, keeps both senses).

anf_compare.notes: Crombie (ANF 1872) and Chadwick (1953) were not used or consulted; English is from the Greek.

translator_notes: The earlier defence citing Phlegon is at Against Celsus 2.14 and 2.33. The clause ‘while he was alive... pierced’ is indirect speech (ὅτι) in Origen but is repeated almost word for word below, so it is marked as Celsus’s wording. ‘So he did not open his mouth’ is the end of Isaiah 53:7 (LXX οὕτως οὐκ ἀνοίγει τὸ στόμα αὐτοῦ); Origen says the Gospel bears witness to it, i.e. Jesus’ silence before his judges (Matthew 26:63; 27:12–14; Mark 15:5). τὰ μέσα is the Stoic term for things morally indifferent, rendered ‘things indifferent’. On ‘as you say’ (ὥς φατε): Celsus may be glancing at Mary Magdalene’s seven demons (Mark 16:9; Luke 8:2); uncertain, so not cited inline. γοητεία rendered ‘sorcery’; the jibe may mean either fellow members of the same band of sorcerers or people under the same spell, so ‘involved in’ is kept open to both.
